paragraphs: By around 160 million years ago the sauropods, the long-necked plant eaters that include Diplodocus, Apatosaurus and Brachiosaurus, had become the largest animals ever to walk on land, some reaching over 30 metres long and more than 50 tonnes. Their size is usually explained by a combination of efficient, bird-like lungs and long necks that let them graze a wide area of vegetation without moving their whole bulk.

Sauropods were not alone at that size for long: sharp-toothed predators such as Allosaurus grew to match the scale of the herds they hunted. The fossil beds that preserve this period best, including North America's Morrison Formation, are read layer by layer to work out which species overlapped in time and which replaced which as the Jurassic wore on.

Palaeontologists nickname the Devonian Period, roughly 419 to 359 million years ago, the Age of Fishes because fish diversity exploded across that stretch: armoured placoderms, early sharks, ray-finned fish and lobe-finned fish all shared the same seas and rivers. The 400 million year mark falls in the middle of that window, close to its most productive fossil beds.

Placoderms, heavily armoured and now entirely extinct, were the dominant predators for much of the period, some growing several metres long with bony plates instead of jaws lined in teeth. It was also lobe-finned fish from this same Devonian world, distinguished by fins built on stubby, muscled limbs rather than simple rays, that would eventually give rise to the first four-legged animals on land.

The skull came first, found by Mary Anning's brother Joseph on the cliffs near Lyme Regis in 1811, when Mary was twelve. It took her roughly another year of careful digging to expose the rest of the five-metre skeleton, work that fell to her because fossil hunting on that unstable coast was the family trade after their father's death left them needing the income it brought.

Naturalists eventually classed the find as Ichthyosaurus, an extinct marine reptile shaped like a dolphin but unrelated to one, and it became one of the specimens that convinced scientists whole categories of animal had lived and died out before humans existed. Anning went on finding plesiosaurs and other marine reptiles along that coast for decades, rarely credited by the men who bought and published on her fossils.

A single fossil feather turned up in 1861 in fine limestone near Solnhofen, Bavaria, reaching naturalist Hermann von Meyer as the first physical evidence that feathered animals existed in the Jurassic. Later that year a nearly complete skeleton emerged from the same quarry, showing wings and feather impressions on a body that otherwise looked reptilian, with teeth and a long bony tail.

Von Meyer named the animal Archaeopteryx lithographica, and its timing, only two years after Darwin's On the Origin of Species, made it look like exactly the transitional fossil that theory predicted. Solnhofen's limestone was fine enough to preserve feather impressions in detail rarely matched elsewhere, which is why the site kept yielding further Archaeopteryx specimens over the following century and a half.

The skeleton nicknamed Ardi was found in Ethiopia's Afar region in 1994, but the fragile bones took an international team fifteen years to excavate, reconstruct and analyse before they were formally described in 2009. About 125 pieces survived, including much of the skull, pelvis, hands and feet, letting researchers judge how the animal moved rather than guessing from a handful of scraps.

Ardi belonged to Ardipithecus ramidus and lived around 4.4 million years ago, making the skeleton older than the famous Australopithecus fossil Lucy by more than a million years. Its pelvis and foot suggest a creature that could walk upright on the ground while still climbing trees efficiently, evidence against the old assumption that upright walking evolved only after human ancestors left forests behind.

Aristotle spent time on Lesbos dissecting and observing marine life firsthand, and his Historia Animalium describes roughly 500 species, grouped by shared traits such as live birth, blood and mode of reproduction rather than by myth or human use. He got a striking amount right, including the observation that dolphins and whales nurse their young and breathe air.

He also got things wrong, believing flies and other small creatures arose spontaneously from decaying matter, and his fixed ladder of nature, ranking species by supposed perfection, held back biology for centuries. Even so, his habit of classifying by observable structure rather than folklore is why later naturalists treated him as the discipline's starting point.

Fossils of millipede-like animals from around 420 million years ago, in the Silurian Period, are among the earliest confirmed evidence of animals living permanently out of water, breathing air through simple tube-like tracheae rather than gills. Trace fossils, tracks and burrows rather than bodies, hint that arthropods may have been making short trips onto damp ground even earlier.

Land offered these small, armoured animals something the crowded Silurian seas did not: no predators yet adapted to catch them there. That advantage did not last. Within tens of millions of years, air breathing and jointed exoskeletons would let arthropods diversify into the spiders, insects and giant millipedes that dominated early land ecosystems long before any vertebrate came ashore.

Physicist Luis Alvarez and his geologist son Walter did not set out to explain the dinosaurs. They were puzzled by a thin clay layer at the boundary between rock from the Cretaceous and the period after it, and in 1980 they reported that this layer worldwide carried unusually high levels of iridium, an element rare on Earth's surface but common in asteroids.

Their conclusion was that a large asteroid struck Earth roughly 66 million years ago, throwing enough debris into the atmosphere to block sunlight for months and collapse food chains worldwide. Many palaeontologists initially resisted the idea, preferring gradual climate change or volcanism, and it took the 1991 identification of a matching crater to swing majority opinion firmly behind the impact.

The Cambrian Period is now dated from 538.8 million years ago, fixed by a rock layer in Newfoundland chosen as the boundary marker. Within perhaps twenty million years of that line, fossil sites such as China's Chengjiang and Canada's Burgess Shale record an explosion of animal body plans: hard shells, compound eyes, jointed limbs and predators built for speed.

Explosion is a fair word only at geological timescales; it still spans millions of years, and genetic studies suggest the underlying animal lineages had already split earlier, quietly, without leaving fossils. What changed at the Cambrian boundary was preservation as much as evolution: animals began building mineralised skeletons, and skeletons are what turn a soft creature into a fossil that survives half a billion years.

A 9,500-year-old grave on Cyprus holds a cat buried near a person, close enough in position that archaeologists read it as a deliberate pairing rather than coincidence, and cats are not native to Cyprus, so someone brought one there by boat. That pushes the bond back earlier than the Egyptian art usually credited with it, into the first farming villages of the Near East.

Grain stores drew rodents, rodents drew wild cats, and the cats that stayed close to people ate well and bred there, which is closer to self-domestication than deliberate taming. Egyptian paintings from around 2000 BCE onward show cats as settled household animals, but the genetic split between wild and domestic cat populations traces back thousands of years before any Egyptian tomb.

Oil company geologists found a circular gravity and magnetic anomaly under the Yucatan Peninsula in the late 1970s while surveying for petroleum, but nobody linked it to extinction until 1991, when Alan Hildebrand and colleagues matched its age and composition to the iridium layer the Alvarez team had identified a decade earlier. The crater, named Chicxulub, spans roughly 180 kilometres.

Drilling into the crater since has recovered rock melted and reformed within minutes of impact, and modelling of the debris it threw up matches the abrupt, worldwide collapse recorded in the fossil layer. The crater's confirmation turned the asteroid impact from a contested hypothesis into the leading explanation for the end of the Cretaceous, though how much a simultaneous burst of volcanism in India contributed remains debated.

Georges Cuvier compared mastodon and mammoth bones against every living elephant species he could find and, in papers read to the French Institute from 1796, showed the skeletons did not match any animal known to be alive. Until then most naturalists assumed such creatures must still exist somewhere unexplored, since a species vanishing entirely seemed to contradict a divinely ordered, unchanging natural world.

Cuvier's method was comparative anatomy: matching tooth shape, jaw structure and limb proportions closely enough to prove these were genuinely distinct, extinct species rather than unusual living elephants. He went on to argue that Earth's history held a whole succession of such vanished faunas, laying groundwork for a science of extinction decades before anyone had a mechanism to explain why species died out.

The bone was a fragment of a pinky finger, found in Denisova Cave in Siberia's Altai Mountains in 2008 and belonging to a girl who died between roughly 74,000 and 82,000 years ago. When geneticists led by Svante Paabo sequenced its DNA in 2010, it matched neither modern humans nor known Neanderthals, revealing an entirely separate lineage of archaic humans that nobody had suspected from bones alone.

Denisovans left almost no other fossil trace, just a few teeth and bone fragments from the same cave, yet their DNA survives today in some Melanesian, Aboriginal Australian and Tibetan populations, at levels of several per cent in places. A gene inherited from them helps modern Tibetans tolerate high-altitude life, a case of an extinct human population's genes still doing practical work in living people.

Richard Owen coined Dinosauria, terrible lizard, in a report on British fossil reptiles published in 1842, grouping Iguanodon, Megalosaurus and Hylaeosaurus together because their vertebrae and heavy, elephant-like limbs set them apart from ordinary lizards and crocodiles. The name is often dated to a lecture Owen gave the year before, since the volume containing his paper is formally the proceedings of that 1841 meeting.

Owen envisioned these animals as bulky, four-legged beasts rather than the agile creatures later skeletons revealed, and he had life-sized concrete models built on that image for London's Crystal Palace grounds, where several still stand. The word stuck long after the reconstruction it was built on did not, and it now covers a group far larger and stranger than the three species Owen first named.

The dodo had no reason to fear anything on Mauritius before 1598, when Dutch sailors made landfall and found a bird with no memory of predators, easy to walk up to and club. The last confirmed sighting is usually placed around 1662, though some accounts push a straggler population into the 1680s, and no skeleton or preserved body survives complete, only scattered bones and a few dried specimens that later rotted away in European collections.

Sailors ate some dodos, but the pigs, rats and monkeys that ships brought ashore did more lasting damage by raiding the ground nests where a female laid a single egg at a time. Within under a century of first contact the species was gone, and it became the standard shorthand for human-caused extinction long before ecologists had a name for the pattern.

Geneticists cannot agree on a single date because dog and wolf DNA kept mixing long after the split began, but most estimates place domestication somewhere between 15,000 and 40,000 years ago, likely in Eurasia rather than one fixed spot. No one bred the first dog on purpose; wolves that tolerated human camps and scavenged scraps had cubs that were calmer still, and each generation drifted further from wild wolves.

The earliest burial that is widely accepted as a dog, not a wolf, comes from Bonn-Oberkassel in Germany, roughly 14,000 years old, where a puppy was buried alongside two people. By the time farming spread, dogs were already working animals: guarding camps, helping hunts, and, everywhere they went, sharing meals with the same species that once just tolerated them nearby.

Geologists put liquid water on Earth by around 4.4 billion years ago, only about 150 million years after the planet formed. The evidence is indirect: tiny zircon crystals from Western Australia, crystallised from magma in contact with water, are the oldest solid material ever dated. No rock from an actual ocean that old survives.

The figure is an inference from mineral chemistry, not a measured shoreline, and estimates for when a stable, planet-wide ocean existed still range by hundreds of millions of years. What is firmer is the mechanism: as the crust cooled below boiling point, water vapour and volcanic outgassing condensed into rain that pooled into basins, some of it plausibly delivered earlier still by icy impactors.

Around 575 million years ago, soft-bodied creatures with no shells, bones or obvious mouths began covering shallow seafloors, preserved today mostly as impressions in sandstone from sites like Newfoundland, Namibia and Russia's White Sea coast. Palaeontologists split this fossil record into three overlapping phases, and 575 million years marks roughly the start of the earliest, the Avalon assemblage.

Nobody agrees on what many of these organisms actually were. Frond-like Fractofusus and quilted Dickinsonia do not map cleanly onto any living animal group, and some researchers still debate whether a few represent animals at all rather than an entirely separate, extinct kind of complex life.

No fossil egg survives from this event. What survives is the animal that could have laid one: Hylonomus, a small lizard-like reptile from Nova Scotia dated to about 318 million years ago, the oldest widely accepted amniote body fossil. The shelled, membrane-lined egg itself is inferred from its skeleton, not preserved, since fossilised amniote eggs do not turn up in rock until the age of dinosaurs, tens of millions of years later.

The timing is being revised outward rather than in. Trackways described in recent years have been read by some researchers as amniote tracks tens of millions of years older than Hylonomus, which would push the true origin of the egg well back into the Carboniferous or earlier. That reading is disputed, and body fossils remain the firmer anchor for when dry-land breeding began.

Proconsul, unearthed from Miocene rock around Lake Victoria in Kenya and Uganda, is usually cited as an early ape, living roughly between 23 and 14 million years ago. It had a monkey-like body built for moving along branches rather than swinging beneath them, but lacked a tail and showed early signs of the more mobile shoulder that later apes rely on for climbing and hanging.

Whether Proconsul belongs on the ape branch of the family tree or just below it, ancestral to both apes and Old World monkeys, is still argued over by researchers who study its teeth and limb bones. That disagreement matters because it shifts exactly where, and how far back, the split that eventually leads toward gorillas, chimpanzees and humans should be drawn.

The oldest known bee is a single male trapped in amber from Myanmar, described in 2006 and dated to about 100 million years ago, some 35 to 45 million years older than any bee fossil found before it. At just under 3 millimetres long it looks like a halfway point between a bee and a wasp, with the branched, pollen-catching hairs of a bee but hind legs closer to a hunting wasp's.

That mix is the fossil's real value: it supports the idea that bees split off from meat-eating wasp ancestors once flowering plants gave them a reliable alternative food source, pollen, worth specialising for. Genetic estimates for when bees actually originated run somewhat earlier than this amber specimen, since a fossil can only mark the oldest confirmed date, never the true first appearance.

By around 485 million years ago, at the start of the Ordovician Period, tabulate and rugose corals had joined sponges and calcified algae in building the first true reef ecosystems, structures large and rigid enough to shelter their own communities of trilobites, brachiopods and early cephalopods. Unlike modern reef corals, none of these builders relied on the algal partnership that colours reefs today.

The Ordovician reef boom followed a burst of biodiversity called the Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event, when marine life diversified sharply after the slower pace of the Cambrian. Those early reefs would later be devastated, along with much else in the oceans, by the extinction that closed the Ordovician around 40 million years afterward, a reminder that reef building on Earth has been interrupted before.

Cherts from the Apex Basalt in Western Australia hold filament-shaped microstructures once described as 3.5 billion year old cyanobacteria, the microbes credited with putting oxygen into the atmosphere. That identification has been argued over for years, with some researchers reading the same structures as mineral artefacts rather than cells.

Confirmed cyanobacterial biomarkers, chemical traces rather than disputed shapes in rock, only reach back to about 2.9 billion years, found in South African shale. The gap between the confident date and the claimed one is the point: cyanobacteria almost certainly existed earlier than the evidence anyone fully trusts, and the 3.5 billion year figure survives as a plausible but contested outer bound.

The oldest well-dated dinosaurs come from a single stretch of rock in northwestern Argentina, the Ischigualasto Formation, laid down about 231 million years ago. Eoraptor was barely the size of a dog and had teeth suited to eating almost anything, while its neighbour Herrerasaurus was a metre-tall predator with a hinged lower jaw for gripping prey, a design later hunting dinosaurs would refine.

Neither animal looked like a ruler of anything. They shared the landscape with far larger non-dinosaur reptiles and amphibians, and dinosaurs stayed a minor part of the fauna for millions of years after this. The dominance usually imagined, and the huge body sizes that go with it, only arrived once a mass extinction near the end of the Triassic cleared out most of the competition.

The title of oldest flowering plant has changed hands more than once. For years the aquatic Archaefructus, dated to about 125 million years ago, held it, until a 2015 study of a weedy Spanish water plant, Montsechia vidalii, argued it was at least as old, around 130 million years, and possibly older. Even calling Montsechia a flowering plant took decades, since it was once classified as a conifer.

Both were unglamorous freshwater weeds, not showy blooms; Montsechia had no petals at all, just a seed enclosed in tissue, the technical feature that defines an angiosperm. Some researchers have proposed even older, Jurassic candidates from China, but those claims remain disputed, and most botanists still place the group's confirmed origin in the Early Cretaceous.

By around 385 million years ago, plants called Archaeopteris had grown into genuine trees, with woody trunks, branching crowns and true roots that spread underground rather than simply anchoring a low mat. Fossil root systems found in New York State show them growing closely enough together to form the first forests, densely enough to change how rivers and soils behaved around them.

Those roots pulled carbon dioxide out of the atmosphere on a new scale, and many researchers link this Devonian greening to a long-term cooling of the climate and to falling oxygen and carbon dioxide levels that reshaped conditions for every organism sharing the planet with them. Archaeopteris itself went extinct by the end of the Devonian, but the rooted, woody body plan it pioneered did not.

Grasses did not wait for the dinosaurs to disappear. Microscopic silica structures called phytoliths, preserved on the teeth of a duck-billed dinosaur in China and in sauropod dung from India, show grasses growing as early as 113 million years ago and still present right up to the extinction 66 million years ago, tens of millions of years before this event's date.

What changed after the extinction was not grass's existence but its reach. Freed from the browsing pressure and shade of Cretaceous forests, and helped by a cooling, drying climate through the following tens of millions of years, grasses expanded from scattered patches into the continuous plains and savannas that later grazing mammals, including horses and antelope, evolved to exploit.

Jaws seem to have evolved from the forward gill arches of jawless fish, hinging a set of supporting rods so they could open and close around prey. Isolated scales assigned to jawed fish push the record back to around 439 million years ago, in the Silurian Period, well before the armoured placoderms and early sharks that make up most later Silurian and Devonian jawed fossils.

The 425 million year mark sits inside that same Silurian stretch, when body fossils of jawed fish, not just scattered scales, start turning up more widely. Molecular comparisons of living species suggest the jaw lineage split even earlier, into the preceding Ordovician Period, so the fossils confirm a milestone that living genes imply happened somewhat earlier still.

A billion years ago is a convenient marker rather than a true starting point: cells cooperating in groups is not one event but something that happened independently, more than once, at very different times. Red algae from Somerset Island in Arctic Canada, dated to around 1.2 billion years ago, already show cells specialised into different roles and even sexual reproduction.

Push earlier and the claims get shakier rather than disappearing. Coin-sized, coordinated colonial structures from Gabon have been dated to 2.1 billion years, and disputed 1.6 billion year old fossils from India have been read as red algae too. None displaces the billion year mark as a rough threshold after which multicellular life becomes common in the rock record, rather than an isolated, arguable trace.

The oldest confirmed primate relative is older than this event's date by roughly ten million years. Purgatorius, a squirrel-sized climber known from teeth and ankle bones found in Montana, has been dated to about 65.9 million years ago, only around 100,000 to 140,000 years after the extinction that killed off the dinosaurs, and some researchers argue its lineage reaches back into the Late Cretaceous itself.

That timing means the ancestors of monkeys, apes and humans lived alongside large dinosaurs rather than appearing only once mammals had the world to themselves. Purgatorius spread and diversified quickly once it did emerge, taking advantage of forests recovering from the extinction, before the grasping hands and forward-facing eyes typical of later primates evolved.

The earliest trilobite fossils appear around 521 million years ago, already carrying a segmented, calcite-armoured body plan good enough that the group would persist, largely unchanged in outline, for another 270 million years. Their compound eyes are among the oldest complex visual systems known, made of the same mineral as their shells.

Because that armour fossilises so readily, trilobites left one of the densest records of any Cambrian animal, which is partly why an exact first appearance keeps shifting slightly as older sites turn up in Morocco, China and Siberia. What holds steady is the pattern: trilobites arrive already diverse rather than as a single ancestral form, implying an unfossilised history that stretches earlier still.

The earliest claimed evidence of upright walking is far older than 4 million years. A femur and forearm bones assigned to Sahelanthropus, found in Chad and dated to about 7 million years old, have been read by some researchers as showing hip and knee joints built for walking on two legs, and a partial thighbone from the roughly 6 million year old Orrorin in Kenya has been argued the same way.

Neither case is settled. Critics point out that the same bones overlap in shape with those of tree-climbing apes, and a handful of fragments cannot show whether an animal walked upright occasionally or as its normal way of moving. Firmer, more complete evidence of habitual bipedalism only arrives later, with Australopithecus species closer to 4 million years old and younger.

Fossils from the Chengjiang site in southern China, dated to roughly 518 million years ago, include Myllokunmingia and Haikouichthys, small eel-like animals with a skull, a notochord and paired sensory structures. They lack a true backbone of vertebrae, so calling them the first vertebrates stretches the word slightly, but they sit close enough to that origin to be treated as the earliest known members of the lineage.

These animals had no bone, no scales in the modern sense and no fins beyond simple flaps, yet the basic vertebrate body plan, a head at one end and a tail-propelled swimming body, was already fixed. Everything with a spine alive today, humans included, traces back through descendants of animals built along that same Chengjiang blueprint.

Tiktaalik, found in rocks from Ellesmere Island in Arctic Canada dated to around 375 million years ago, had a fish's scales and gills alongside a flattened head, a mobile neck and front fins containing wrist-like bones, features useful in shallow water rather than on dry ground. It is usually described as an animal that could prop itself up in shallows, not one that walked on land.

Tracks in Polish rock, dated slightly earlier at around 395 million years, appear to show a four-legged animal already walking, which complicates any tidy story of gradual transition and suggests the move onto land happened over a longer, messier stretch than one iconic fossil can show. Tiktaalik remains the clearest illustration of the anatomical steps involved, even if it was not, strictly, the first.

Ground sloths were not a single species but a whole family, some no bigger than a large dog and others, like Megatherium, standing taller than an elephant on their hind legs to strip leaves from high branches. They evolved in South America and spread north once a land bridge connected the continents, roaming as far as what is now the United States long before the most recent Ice Age began.

Fossil trackways and dung deposits, some preserved dry in caves for tens of thousands of years, show they survived multiple glacial cycles before the last populations vanished around 11,000 years ago alongside most other American megafauna. Sloth skin fragments recovered from Patagonian caves still carry osteoderms, bony deposits in the hide that gave the living animal something like natural armour.

Meganeura, a griffinfly often mistaken for a dragonfly, had a wingspan approaching 75 centimetres, the largest insect known to have flown. Its size is usually credited to Carboniferous air running roughly 30 to 35 percent oxygen, well above today's 21 percent, on the reasoning that insects breathe through tubes called tracheae and more oxygen let those tubes feed a bigger body.

That explanation has been challenged. Later griffinfly relatives of similar size turn up in the Permian, after oxygen had already fallen, and lab work suggests tracheae are more adaptable to low oxygen than the theory assumed. Researchers now suspect open sky with few flying predators, rather than the air itself, gave these insects room to grow so large before birds and their competitors evolved.

Geologists cannot agree on a single date for this collision, because India did not hit Asia cleanly and all at once. Some sediment records put initial contact around 59 million years ago; other studies place the two continental plates fully together closer to 40 million years ago. The mismatch partly comes from the plates meeting at different times along the range's length.

Whatever the exact date, India kept pushing after contact, since its plate was moving unusually fast for continental crust. Rather than sliding beneath Asia the way ocean floor normally does, the two continents' relatively light, thick crust crumpled and stacked upward instead of sinking, and that stacking is still adding height today, roughly a centimetre or two each year.

The clearest early evidence for organised beekeeping is Egyptian: managed colonies kept in cylindrical clay or mud pipes stacked in rows, shown in a relief from the sun temple of Niuserre near Abusir, roughly 2400 BCE. This went well beyond gathering honey from wild hives. Beekeepers smoked the hives to move the bees, then harvested honey and wax without destroying the colony each time.

Honey was Egypt's main sweetener and preservative, and wax went into cosmetics, medicine and the sealing of documents, while temple and tomb texts record honey used in offerings to the gods. Wild honey hunting is far older, painted on rock shelters thousands of years before, but the Abusir relief is the earliest clear record of bees kept deliberately, in a fixed place, for repeated harvest.

There is no single agreed date for this split, because there is no fossil of the shared ancestor itself, only genetic estimates and fossils on either side of the divide. Molecular clocks long favoured roughly 5 to 6 million years ago, but fossils such as Sahelanthropus and Orrorin, both dated to 6 to 7 million years old and argued by many researchers to sit on the human branch, pushed the working estimate back closer to 7 million years.

The disagreement runs deeper than the date. Some geneticists and anthropologists doubt Sahelanthropus and Orrorin belong on the human lineage at all, arguing their humanlike traits could have evolved separately rather than through shared descent, which is why textbooks still hedge this split across a range rather than a year.

James Hutton, a Scottish farmer and naturalist, presented his theory to the Royal Society of Edinburgh in 1785, arguing that the slow processes still visible today, erosion and uplift, had always operated and needed far more time than the Bible's chronology allowed. At Siccar Point on the Scottish coast he found rock layers tilted almost vertical beneath others lying flat, proof of a gap between two separate periods of deposition.

Looking at that unconformity, Hutton is said to have remarked that he found no vestige of a beginning, no prospect of an end. The claim scandalised readers used to a world only a few thousand years old, but John Playfair's clearer retelling of Hutton's ideas carried them further and gave geology room to work in millions rather than thousands of years.

The die-off was not a single event but a long, uneven collapse, with most large mammal losses in the Americas, Europe and Australia clustered between roughly 50,000 and 10,000 years ago and still running when farming began. Mammoths, sabre-toothed cats, giant sloths and the woolly rhinoceros disappeared from most of their range within that stretch.

Researchers still argue over how much weight to give warming climate against the arrival of human hunters carrying new weapons, and the balance shifts by continent: Australia's losses came earlier and align more with people, while North America's align more with the end of the last glaciation. Small mammoth populations on Arctic islands such as Wrangel survived until about 4,000 years ago, long after the mainland herds were gone.

Louis Agassiz had studied glaciers in his native Switzerland, tracking boulders and scratched bedrock far from any current ice, before arguing to the Swiss Society of Natural Sciences in 1837 that a single vast ice sheet had once covered much of northern Europe. Most geologists at the time explained scattered boulders and grooved rock by a great flood carrying debris, not by ice that had since melted away.

Agassiz extended the theory after visiting Britain and North America, reading the same telltale scratches and displaced rock into the landscape there. His idea met heavy resistance for years, but it gradually replaced flood-based explanations and gave geologists their first working picture of repeated ice ages shaping the northern continents long before written history.

Eugene Dubois had gone to the Dutch East Indies as an army surgeon specifically to hunt for a missing link, convinced Asia rather than Africa held the earliest humans. In 1891 his workers found a skullcap on the bank of the Solo River in Java, followed by a thighbone nearby that looked capable of walking upright, and Dubois named the find Pithecanthropus erectus.

Other scientists spent years disputing whether the bones even belonged together, let alone whether they were human, ape or something between. The fossil is now classified as Homo erectus, a species that eventually spread across Africa and Asia and used fire and stone tools, and Java Man's discovery pushed the known age of upright-walking humans back by hundreds of thousands of years.

The last aurochs was a female, and she died of apparently natural causes in the Jaktorow Forest near Warsaw in 1627, not of a hunter's shot. Polish kings had tried to protect the herd for a century, appointing gamekeepers and fining poachers, but a wild population reduced to a handful of animals in one forest had nowhere left to fail safely once disease or a bad winter caught up with it.

Aurochs had once ranged from Britain to China and stood taller at the shoulder than most modern cattle, which descend from them through domestication roughly ten thousand years ago. The skull of this last individual was later carried off by the Swedish army during their invasion of Poland in the 1650s and now sits in the Royal Armoury in Stockholm, the closest thing left to a physical record of the species.

The last known quagga, a female, had lived at Amsterdam's Natura Artis Magistra zoo since 1867 and died there on 12 August 1883. Nobody at the time marked the date as significant; quaggas were assumed to still exist somewhere in the South African interior, and it took decades for naturalists to accept that the zoo animal had been the final one.

A quagga looked like a zebra whose stripes faded out toward the hindquarters into a plain brown coat, and it was hunted hard after Dutch and British settlers expanded into its Karoo grassland range. Only about two dozen preserved specimens survive in museums worldwide, and DNA extracted from them later confirmed it was a subspecies of the plains zebra rather than a separate species.

The last known thylacine, a male nicknamed Benjamin, died at Hobart Zoo in Tasmania on 7 September 1936, reportedly after being locked out of its sheltered sleeping quarters overnight. Tasmania had only removed the government bounty on the animal, paid for decades to farmers who killed it as a supposed sheep-killer, some months earlier.

Despite its nickname the thylacine was a marsupial, not a canine, carrying its young in a pouch and sharing only a superficial resemblance to a dog through convergent evolution. It had already vanished from mainland Australia thousands of years before Europeans arrived, likely outcompeted by dingoes, and survived only in Tasmania until bounty hunting, habitat clearing and disease finished it off there too.

The Late Devonian extinction was not a single blow but a sequence of die-offs spread across several million years, with the sharpest pulse, the Kellwasser event, falling around 372 million years ago. Reef-building organisms were hit hardest: tabulate and rugose corals and stromatoporoids that had built Devonian reef systems mostly disappeared, and reef building did not recover to a similar scale for tens of millions of years.

The likely trigger was widespread ocean oxygen loss, probably driven by nutrient runoff from the newly forested continents feeding algal blooms that stripped oxygen from the water as they decayed. Placoderms, the armoured fish that had dominated Devonian seas, never fully recovered from the losses and were gone entirely by the period's end.

Apollo astronauts brought back lunar rocks that cluster oddly around 3.9 billion years old, and for decades that clustering was read as a spike: a late surge of asteroids and comets slamming into the young Earth and Moon after things had already calmed down. The idea even got a name, the lunar cataclysm.

The spike is now widely doubted. The Apollo samples came from a small patch of the Moon, much of it near one giant basin, so the cluster may just reflect where astronauts happened to land rather than a solar system wide event. Lunar meteorites collected on Earth, blasted at random from all over the Moon, show ages spread evenly rather than bunched at 3.9 billion years, favouring a slow decline in impacts instead of a sudden bombardment.

Lucy was found in 1974 at Hadar, Ethiopia, and dated to about 3.2 million years ago, an Australopithecus afarensis about a metre tall with roughly 40 percent of her skeleton recovered, unusually complete for a fossil this old. Her name comes not from science but from a song playing at the celebration on the night of the discovery, Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds.

Her hip and knee bones show a gait built for walking upright, much like a modern human's, while her skull stayed small and ape-like and her long, curved fingers still suited climbing trees. That combination was the strongest evidence at the time that walking upright evolved well before large brains did, reversing what many researchers had assumed about which trait came first.

Charles Lyell published the first volume of Principles of Geology in 1830, arguing for uniformitarianism: that the ordinary forces still shaping the world, rivers, volcanoes, erosion, slow uplift, were sufficient to explain its whole history given enough time, without invoking sudden catastrophes. He built the book largely from his own fieldwork, including volcanic terrain in Sicily and the Auvergne.

Charles Darwin carried a copy of Principles aboard the Beagle and later credited it with reshaping how he read landscapes and, eventually, how he thought about the slow accumulation of biological change. Lyell revised the book through many editions over the following decades, and it became the standard geology text for a generation, even as he himself remained cautious for years about accepting evolution.

Stanley Miller was a doctoral student when he built the apparatus in 1952 under Harold Urey's supervision at the University of Chicago, sealing water, methane, ammonia and hydrogen into a glass loop meant to mimic Earth's early atmosphere and ocean. Electrodes sparked the gas mixture continuously to stand in for lightning, and after about a week the liquid had turned pink, then dark red, laced with amino acids.

The experiment did not create life or even a self-replicating molecule, but it showed that the basic building blocks of proteins could form from simple inorganic chemistry given plausible early-Earth conditions and a source of energy. Later reanalysis of Miller's sealed vials found even more amino acid types than his 1953 paper had reported, using far more sensitive instruments.

Geologists call the impactor Theia, after the mythical mother of the moon goddess in Greek legend, though no trace of it survives as something separate from Earth. Apollo astronauts brought home lunar rock that is nearly identical, isotope for isotope, to Earth's own mantle, not the roughly even blend of two different bodies that simple impact models predict.

The newborn Moon also sat far closer to Earth than it does now, and a day on the young planet may have lasted only four to six hours. Tidal drag between the two bodies has pushed the Moon outward ever since, about 3.8 centimetres a year, and slowed Earth's spin as it goes; the 24 hour day is a comparatively recent arrangement.

Quarry workers cutting limestone in the Neander Valley near Dusseldorf found bones in a small cave, the Kleine Feldhofer Grotte, in August 1856: a skullcap, ribs, part of a pelvis and both thighbones, lying about sixty centimetres deep in clay sediment. The workers assumed they belonged to a bear and nearly discarded them before a quarry foreman salvaged the pieces.

A local schoolteacher and fossil collector, Johann Carl Fuhlrott, recognised the bones as unusual and had them examined by the anatomist Hermann Schaaffhausen, who in 1857 argued they belonged to an ancient, distinct human type rather than a diseased modern skeleton or an injured soldier, both explanations others preferred. The find gave the species its name and became the first fossil widely accepted as evidence of an extinct human relative.

Sudan was already the last male northern white rhino when keepers at the Ol Pejeta Conservancy in Kenya put him down on 19 March 2018, aged about 45, after age-related infections and organ failure left no realistic hope of recovery. He had spent his final years under armed guard against poachers, his horn worth more by weight on illegal markets than gold.

Only two northern white rhinos are left, both female, Sudan's daughter and granddaughter, and neither can carry a pregnancy naturally. Scientists have instead frozen sperm from Sudan and other now-dead males and are trying to grow embryos using eggs from the survivors, implanted into southern white rhino surrogates, the subspecies' only realistic route back from what conservationists already call functional extinction.

The Dresser Formation in the Pilbara region of Western Australia holds domed, layered rock structures dated to roughly 3.45 billion years ago, built up as thin sheets of microbes trapped sediment and minerals one film at a time. They are among the oldest deposits anyone still credits as the work of living things.

That credit took decades to settle. Geologists have argued over whether the layering was shaped by microbial mats or just by mineral precipitation and weathering, since heat and pressure over billions of years erase the chemical traces that would settle the question outright. Comparisons with living stromatolites in places like Shark Bay have shifted opinion toward a biological origin, though not to unanimous agreement.

Mary Leakey found the key pieces at Olduvai Gorge in Tanzania in 1959, a heavily built hominin skull she and Louis Leakey initially named Zinjanthropus, unearthed alongside simple stone flakes and choppers. The tools, later classed as Oldowan technology, were made by striking one stone against another to knock off sharp flakes for cutting meat and cracking bone.

The gorge's layered sediments let the Leakeys date the find using new potassium-argon techniques, and the tools came out far older than anyone had expected, around 1.75 million years. The skull itself is now attributed to a different, heavily built genus, Paranthropus, but the site reset the timeline for when toolmaking began and shifted the search for human origins firmly onto East Africa.

The Late Ordovician mass extinction, centred around 445 million years ago, killed an estimated 85 percent of marine species during a period when almost all life lived in the sea. It arrived in two pulses rather than one blow, separated by roughly a million years, and the leading explanation is a sharp cooling of the climate as glaciers spread across the southern supercontinent Gondwana.

The cooling lowered sea levels and drained the shallow shelf habitats where trilobites, brachiopods and early corals were most crowded together, and a second pulse tied to spreading low oxygen water in the oceans finished the job. It ranks among the largest of the five events usually called the big mass extinctions, and it happened without any known asteroid impact or volcanic trigger.

The split did not open along one clean seam. Rifting through the Late Triassic widened into full separation around 175 million years ago, when magma welling up through weakened crust tore Laurasia in the north away from Gondwana in the south. The narrow gap that resulted became the first sliver of the central Atlantic Ocean, running between what is now northwestern Africa and North America.

The breakup then stalled and restarted for tens of millions of years rather than proceeding in one steady drift. A second major phase, in the Early Cretaceous around 150 to 140 million years ago, pulled Gondwana itself apart into Africa, South America, India and the linked mass of Antarctica and Australia, the arrangement that eventually settled into today's map.

Pangaea was not one collision but a long series of them. The process began around 335 million years ago as Gondwana and Euramerica drifted together, and geologists generally place the supercontinent's essential completion much later, around 300 million years ago in the early Permian, once the final landmasses had sutured shut. The single ocean around it, Panthalassa, was larger than any ocean today.

The joins are still visible. The collision that closed the gap between what is now Africa and North America threw up the Appalachian and Atlas mountains, worn stumps of a range that once rivalled the Himalayas. Rock strata and matching fossil plants on continents now separated by ocean are read as evidence of exactly where those pieces once locked together.

Martha, the last known passenger pigeon, died in her cage at the Cincinnati Zoo on 1 September 1914. She had lived there alone for years after her last companions died, with a reward once offered for a wild mate that nobody ever collected, because there was none left to find.

The species had numbered in the billions in the early 1800s, flocks so vast that observers described them darkening the sky for hours as they passed overhead. Commercial hunters shipped the birds to city markets by the trainload through the late nineteenth century, and because the pigeons bred and roosted communally in huge, exposed colonies, the population collapsed within a few decades rather than declining gradually.

Pasteur's proof was a pair of swan-necked flasks. Broth boiled in a flask with a straight neck went cloudy with microbes within days; broth in a flask whose neck curved so dust could not reach the liquid stayed sterile for years, because the curve trapped airborne germs while still letting air through. The French Academy of Sciences had put up a prize in 1860 for whoever settled the question either way, and Pasteur claimed it in 1862.

The idea he was up against, spontaneous generation, held that maggots, mould and microbes arose directly from decaying matter rather than from other living things. It had already lost ground after Francesco Redi's 1668 experiments with sealed meat jars, but Pasteur's flasks closed the case for microorganisms, and underpinned the germ theory he built over the following decades.

The earliest solid evidence of land plants is chemical rather than a visible fossil: spore-like grains called cryptospores, coated in a resistant polymer that only survives outside water, appear in rocks from around 470 million years ago. No stems, leaves or roots are attached to them; they simply prove something plant-like was reproducing on dry ground.

Whatever produced those spores would have looked nothing like a plant today, probably a low mat resembling liverworts, without a vascular system to carry water upward. That limitation meant the earliest land plants stayed small and close to damp ground for tens of millions of years, until later innovations such as roots and rigid stems allowed true forests to rise.

Smilodon fatalis, the best-known saber-toothed cat, ranged across the Americas from roughly 700,000 years ago until its extinction around 10,000 to 11,000 years ago, a longer and later span than a single origin date can capture. Built like a lion but heavier, up to about 280 kilograms, it carried canine teeth as long as 18 centimetres, too fragile for the bone-crushing bite of a modern big cat.

Thousands of its skeletons come from one place, the Rancho La Brea asphalt seeps in Los Angeles, where trapped prey animals lured predators into tar pits that then preserved both in extraordinary numbers. Healed fractures on many of those skeletons, injuries that would have needed weeks of feeding without hunting, are the main evidence that Smilodon lived and hunted in social groups.

Fred Vine and Drummond Matthews, using survey data from the Indian Ocean's Carlsberg Ridge, published their explanation in 1963: magnetic minerals in fresh seafloor rock lock in the direction of Earth's magnetic field as they cool, and the field periodically flips polarity. That produces mirror-image stripes of alternating magnetism spreading out symmetrically from a mid-ocean ridge.

The stripes only make sense if new crust is continuously forming at the ridge and pushing older crust outward on both sides, which is exactly what Harry Hess had proposed as seafloor spreading a couple of years earlier without hard proof. The magnetic pattern gave that idea the evidence it needed and became one of the strongest pillars of plate tectonics as it became accepted later in the 1960s.

Shen Kuo was a Song dynasty official and polymath, not a specialist naturalist, who noted in his 1088 notebook Dream Pool Essays that petrified bamboo shoots had been found deep underground in a dry northern region where bamboo could not then grow. He reasoned that the climate there must once have been wetter and warmer, so the land itself had changed over time.

He made a similar argument from marine shells and fish-like fossils embedded in rock cliffs far from any sea, concluding they marked an ancient coastline that had shifted inland. Western geology reached comparable conclusions about slow environmental change only centuries later, making Shen Kuo's brief, almost incidental notebook entry an early and independent statement of the idea.

The moth behind silk, Bombyx mori, can no longer fly, see well, or survive without help; thousands of years of selective breeding for thread quality left it entirely dependent on people, unlike almost every other domesticated animal. Chinese silk fragments and tools for reeling thread date back past 3500 BCE, with legend crediting a Neolithic empress named Leizu for noticing that boiled cocoons unravelled into a single fine strand.

Each cocoon can yield close to a kilometre of continuous filament, which is why silk stayed a closely guarded craft: production methods were kept inside China for millennia, and revealing them to outsiders reportedly carried a death sentence. Silk eventually travelled west along trade routes that took the fabric's name, though the insect itself never spread beyond human care.

William Smith worked as a surveyor on canal and mining projects across England, and the travel let him notice that the same rock layers always held the same distinctive fossils in the same order, wherever he found them exposed. That let him identify a stratum from its fossils alone, even where the rock itself looked similar to a neighbouring layer.

In 1815 he published a hand-coloured map covering England, Wales and part of Scotland showing the strata across the whole country, the first geological map at that scale anywhere. Wealthier geologists initially dismissed the self-taught surveyor's work and some copied it without credit, leaving Smith in debtor's prison for a time before the Geological Society later recognised him with its first Wollaston Medal.

Nicolas Steno was a Danish anatomist working in Florence when his 1669 treatise on solid bodies set out what became the law of superposition: rock layers form as horizontal sheets stacked in the order they were deposited, oldest at the bottom, unless later disturbed. He had been dissecting a shark's head and comparing its teeth to so-called tongue stones, concluding the stones were fossilised teeth, not mineral growths.

From that single comparison he built a general argument that layered rock recorded a sequence of past events readable like pages, given how they were laid down. Steno left science soon after for the priesthood, but his short book gave later geologists the basic tool for reading relative age from rock layers, well before anyone could measure age in years.

Marjorie Courtenay-Latimer, a museum curator in East London, South Africa, went to look through a trawler's catch on 23 December 1938 and found a strange blue fish with limb-like fins among the sharks. She could not identify it and eventually preserved what she could before the flesh spoiled in the heat, then sent a sketch to the ichthyologist J.L.B. Smith, who recognised it as a coelacanth.

Coelacanths were known only from fossils up to roughly 400 million years old and had been assumed extinct since the age of dinosaurs. Smith spent weeks searching the coast before a second specimen turned up years later off the Comoro Islands, confirming a living population survived in deep water. The fish's fins move in a limb-like pattern that has made it useful for studying how fish first evolved toward walking on land.

Cross a narrow strait between Bali and Lombok and the animals change abruptly: tigers, monkeys and woodpeckers give way to marsupials and cockatoos, even though the islands sit only twenty miles apart and the climate barely differs. Alfred Russel Wallace charted this boundary in 1859 while collecting specimens across the Malay Archipelago, tracing it north between Borneo and Sulawesi to separate a distinctly Asian fauna from an Australian one.

The line marks where a deep ocean trench kept the two landmasses apart even when ice-age sea levels fell low enough to join shallower straits into dry land bridges. Wallace was working out evolutionary ideas in parallel with Darwin, and had already pushed Darwin to publish; the line named after him remains a working boundary in biogeography rather than a historical curiosity.

Pakicetus, the earliest known whale ancestor, did not look aquatic at all. About the size of a large dog, it lived on the banks of rivers and lakes in what is now Pakistan roughly 50 million years ago, hunted on four legs, and is classified as a whale mainly on the strength of its inner ear, already tuned for hearing underwater the way its aquatic descendants would.

The switch to full ocean life happened fast by evolutionary standards. Within about ten million years its descendants, including the amphibious Ambulocetus with flipper-like feet, had moved from wading predator to fully marine mammal, trading legs for flukes and a nose that migrated up the skull into a blowhole, a change traced almost bone by bone across intermediate fossils.

The woolly mammoth is usually said to have emerged in East Asia around 400,000 years ago, though genetic and skeletal studies push its split from the earlier steppe mammoth back further, somewhere between 800,000 and 600,000 years ago, so the figure is a rough marker rather than a fixed birthday. Either way it descends from a long chain of mammoth species stretching back millions of years, well before the Ice Age it is now identified with.

Small ears, a thick fat layer and a coat of long guard hair over dense wool let it hold heat on the open steppe, and dung, hair and whole frozen carcasses recovered from Siberian permafrost preserve those adaptations directly rather than as guesswork from bone alone. The last known population survived in isolation on Russia's Wrangel Island until roughly 4,000 years ago.
